epics.title: Switchboard — service control plane
epics.description:
Owner: Daniel. Status: proposed, not started. Discussed 2026-08-06. Twenty to fifty containers across several hosts, plus bare-metal services (skippy.service), plus remote minds (Hex on Sentinel, the Windows kid boxes). Today the state of all of it lives in Daniel's head and in ad-hoc docker ps output. Portainer was installed once and abandoned, because Portainer lists containers — it never says which ones are wrong, and a list of fifty healthy-looking rows is not a tool.

The valuable half of this idea is the judgment layer, not the UI. A container needs attention because its image is newer than the running one, its config file changed after it booted, it has been unhealthy for ten minutes, or it is holding a stale mount. Those are rules that produce findings with reasons attached. The page is a queue of findings with a button on each. Build the rules first and the page is trivial; build the page first and it is Portainer with worse auth.
epics.requirements:
Core model: managed targets, not containers. The unit is a managed target with an adapter behind it — same row shape, different executor: docker_local for a container in a compose stack on this workstation, docker_ssh for a container on another host, systemd_local for a unit on this host, systemd_ssh and winrm_task for a unit or scheduled task on a remote box, and mind for a target whose adapter is another mind (Hex manages his own host, so the switchboard asks him rather than reaching in). Hive containers are discovered and registered by default; everything else is a bolt-on the user adds explicitly, with credentials and a health check declared at add time.

The executor must not live inside anything it can restart: a small host-level systemd unit with a local socket, not a container and not part of hive-comms. The web page is a client; the executor does the work and survives everything it touches, including skippy.service. Self-restart already works today, detached so the command outlives its own parent — the comms-down-then-skippy-down incident was not a timing bug, it was a missing dependency graph. So every target declares dependencies and a health check at registration time, non-negotiable, and a bolt-on without them is rejected, because an unhealthy-but-unknown dependency is exactly how the deadlock happened. The executor walks a plan in dependency order and gates on health checks rather than sleeps — skippy waits on comms healthy, comms waits on lucent healthy. Plans are transactional enough to report per-step outcome, and a failed gate halts the remainder rather than charging on.

Scope is every service Daniel wants to control, not just the hive: splitting hive things here and everything else there is a usability step down, and the recent work already crossed that line repeatedly. Open question whether the UI is a section of the hive console or a page on the owner site; the executor's placement is fixed either way. Related: Hex's Loki poller is the natural source for unhealthy findings, so do not stand up a second poller; and bolt-on targets need credentials, so reuse the credential rotation console's registry rather than inventing a parallel one.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Minds queue work here, which is the point rather than a side effect. When Skippy rebuilds the comms image he does not message Daniel on Telegram asking permission to restart it — he writes a finding and a proposed plan into the same queue the probes write to, and Daniel sees it on the page with an approve button. That is a better inter-mind protocol than a conversational ask, because it is durable, inspectable, batched, and it survives the session ending.
epics.qa_tests: Per phase. The dependency-graph property is the one with history behind it: a restart plan must gate on health checks rather than sleeps, and a failed gate must halt the remainder. The comms-down-then-skippy-down deadlock is the concrete failure to test against.

features.title: Phase 1 — read-only truth
features.description: The rules first. No buttons.
features.requirements: A target registry with hive containers auto-discovered and a bolt-on schema carrying adapter, credentials reference, dependencies and health check. Probes for unhealthy, image_stale and image_reclaim. A findings queue as a read-only page.
features.acceptance_criteria: Every finding carries a target, a reason in plain language, a proposed action and a severity.
features.qa_tests: A container whose image digest differs from the newest local tag produces an image_stale finding naming both. A healthy container produces none. A bolt-on registered without dependencies or a health check is rejected.

stories.title: Build the target registry with auto-discovery and a bolt-on schema
stories.description: Hive containers discovered and registered by default; everything else added explicitly with credentials and a health check declared at add time.
stories.requirements: Adapter, credentials reference, dependencies and health check per bolt-on. A bolt-on missing dependencies or a health check is rejected.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No target exists without a declared health check and dependency set.
stories.qa_tests: A bolt-on without dependencies is refused at registration. An unhealthy-but-unknown dependency is exactly how the deadlock happened, which is why this is non-negotiable rather than a default.

stories.title: Write the unhealthy, image_stale and image_reclaim probes
stories.description: unhealthy means a failing healthcheck or a restart loop. image_stale means the running container's image digest differs from the newest local tag or from the registry. image_reclaim means dangling and unreferenced images, with size attached.
stories.requirements: Each probe emits findings with a reason attached, not a status.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A finding says why, in plain language.
stories.qa_tests: Each probe fires on a constructed condition and stays silent otherwise. image_reclaim reports size, because approving twenty gigs of reclamation should feel identical to approving a restart.

stories.title: Add the config_drift and stale_mount probes
stories.description: config_drift means a bind-mounted config or .env has an mtime later than the container's start time. stale_mount means a mounted source path no longer exists or was replaced.
stories.requirements: Both compared against the container's actual start time and actual mounts.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A config edited after boot is surfaced.
stories.qa_tests: Touching a bind-mounted .env after a container starts produces config_drift. Replacing a mount source produces stale_mount.

stories.title: Render the findings queue read-only
stories.description: A queue of findings. No buttons yet.
stories.requirements: Target, reason, proposed action and severity per row.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The page says which things are wrong, not which things exist.
stories.qa_tests: A healthy fleet renders an empty queue — which is the difference from Portainer.

features.title: Phase 2 — executor
features.description: The executor must not live inside anything it can restart.
features.requirements: A host-level systemd unit with a socket API, outside every stack. A dependency graph walk with health gating. Restart and rebuild actions for docker_local. The approve button wired to plans.
features.acceptance_criteria: The executor survives everything it touches, including skippy.service.
features.qa_tests: Restarting skippy.service through the executor does not kill the executor. A plan whose first health gate fails halts rather than charging on.

stories.title: Stand up the executor as a host-level systemd unit with a socket API
stories.description: Not a container, not part of hive-comms. The web page is a client.
stories.requirements: Outside every stack it can act on.
stories.acceptance_criteria: It survives restarting anything it manages.
stories.qa_tests: Restarting the whole docker stack leaves the executor running. Restarting skippy.service does too.

stories.title: Walk plans in dependency order, gating on health checks rather than sleeps
stories.description: skippy waits on comms healthy; comms waits on lucent healthy. The comms-down-then-skippy-down incident was a missing dependency graph, not a timing bug.
stories.requirements: Health gates, never sleeps. A failed gate halts the remainder.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A dependency that never comes healthy stops the plan rather than producing a broken restart.
stories.qa_tests: With lucent held down, a plan to restart skippy halts at the comms gate and reports which step failed. Per-step outcomes are reported rather than one aggregate result.

stories.title: Add restart and rebuild actions for docker_local and wire the approve button
stories.description: The first adapter to get write actions.
stories.requirements: Approve runs a plan; the plan reports per-step outcome.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A finding can be acted on from the page.
stories.qa_tests: Approving an image_stale finding rebuilds and restarts in dependency order. A failure reports which step and stops.

features.title: Phase 3 — beyond this host
features.description: The remaining adapters, including the one that delegates to another mind.
features.requirements: docker_ssh and systemd_ssh adapters, with credentials handled through the credential rotation console rather than a second secret store. systemd_local for skippy.service, which is the self-restart case. A mind adapter that delegates to Hex for Sentinel rather than reaching in.
features.acceptance_criteria: A service on another machine is manageable from the same queue, and Hex's host is asked rather than reached into.
features.qa_tests: A restart of a remote container works through the SSH adapter with credentials drawn from the rotation console. A Sentinel target routes to Hex rather than opening an SSH session.

stories.title: Add the docker_ssh and systemd_ssh adapters
stories.description: Credentials through the credential rotation console, not a second secret store.
stories.requirements: One credential registry, reused.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A remote target works without a parallel secret store.
stories.qa_tests: A remote restart succeeds using a credential the rotation console holds. No second store exists.

stories.title: Add systemd_local for skippy.service
stories.description: The self-restart case. Already works today, detached so the command outlives its own parent.
stories.requirements: The executor survives it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: skippy.service restarts and the executor is still up.
stories.qa_tests: A restart completes and the executor reports its outcome, which it could not do if it died with the target.

stories.title: Add the mind adapter so Hex manages Sentinel
stories.description: The switchboard asks him rather than reaching in.
stories.requirements: A target whose adapter is another mind.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Sentinel work is delegated, not performed remotely.
stories.qa_tests: A Sentinel finding's plan sends Hex a request rather than opening a connection to .16.

features.title: Phase 4 — minds as producers
features.description: The point of the whole design: a mind queues work rather than asking on Telegram.
features.requirements: An authenticated finding-submission endpoint for minds. proposed_by_mind findings render with the mind's stated reason. Retire the 'may I restart X' Telegram ask in favour of the queue.
features.acceptance_criteria: A rebuilt image produces a queued finding with a proposed plan, not a conversational ask.
features.qa_tests: Skippy rebuilding the comms image produces a proposed_by_mind finding carrying his reason. The Telegram ask no longer happens. Durable, inspectable, batched, and surviving the session ending are the four properties that make this better than the ask — the last one is testable by killing the session and finding the row still there.

stories.title: Add an authenticated finding-submission endpoint for minds
stories.description: Minds write into the same queue the probes write to.
stories.requirements: Authenticated, so a finding's author is known.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A mind's finding is attributable.
stories.qa_tests: A submitted finding names the submitting mind. An unauthenticated submission is refused.

stories.title: Render proposed_by_mind findings with the mind's stated reason
stories.description: So Daniel reads why rather than what.
stories.requirements: The reason travels with the finding.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The page shows the mind's own words.
stories.qa_tests: A submitted finding's reason appears on the page verbatim.

stories.title: Retire the 'may I restart X' Telegram ask
stories.description: Replaced by the queue, which is durable, inspectable, batched, and survives the session ending.
stories.requirements: The standing rules point at the queue instead of the ask.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No mind asks on Telegram for a restart.
stories.qa_tests: A rebuild produces a queued finding and no Telegram message. The row survives the session ending, which the ask never did.

epics.title: App Monitoring Agent
epics.description: Owner: Daniel. Status: proposed, not started. The unified logging standard gives every hive process structured JSON events with a stable vocabulary — session.spawned, http.request.failed, broker.wakeup.failed and the rest — which is the missing precondition for automated log watching; before it, logs were unstructured per-container text with no queryable signal. Loki itself and a 15-minute poll loop already exist: Hex runs both today, with five sources flowing (auth, docker, journald, suricata, zeek), and respond-to-netsage-alert and sentinel-decide poll every 15 minutes and already escalate security findings to Skippy via send-message-to-mind with request_type=security_remediation. Do not stand up a second poller.
epics.requirements: Four parts. First, wire app logs into the same Loki: ship the structured JSON logs from hive-mind services into Hex's Loki alongside the existing host sources, so service=hive-comms, hive-lucent and the rest sit next to source=auth, docker, journald, suricata, zeek. One log backend, one poller. Second, Hex keeps polling and gains a second classification lane, gated on one deterministic field — level. The existing security loop (netsage_run.py, sentinel-triage, sentinel-investigate, sentinel-decide) stays exactly as it is; do not touch it. For app errors, do not write a second text heuristic like pick_anomalies()'s regex — every structured record already carries level WARNING or ERROR, which is hive_logging.py's whole point. That is the same kind of cheap structural gate netsage_run.py already uses for Suricata (severity<=2) and journald (PRIORITY<=4): a LogQL filter over the trailing 15 minutes, dispatching a wake to Hex only when it returns at least one line, same as today rather than an unconditional wake. Hex still makes the judgment call — routine versus security-shaped versus app-error-shaped — in the skill layer once woken, using the event vocabulary as reference; the deterministic gate only decides whether to wake him, not what he decides once woken. Third, route: security-shaped to Skippy as today; app-error-shaped to Argus (new mind, working name, Daniel can rename) with request_type=app_error carrying a correlation id, a log excerpt and the affected service and mind_id; ambiguous or spanning-both to both, with the same correlation id so Daniel does not get two uncorrelated pings about one incident. Fourth, Argus is a receiver rather than a poller: no Loki access and no 15-minute loop of its own, waking on a broker message from Hex, diagnosing the named repo or service, proposing a fix, opening a PR through the same stages the orchestrator already runs, then notifying Daniel via Telegram with a summary, the PR link and an explicit apply-or-hold question. It never auto-merges.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Why this split rather than Argus polling itself: one Loki poller rather than two, avoiding duplicate queries and two places that could disagree about what is new since the last poll. Hex already has the classifier and the security escalation path built and proven, so extending it with one more lane is smaller than building a second classifier in a new mind. It keeps Argus's scope narrow and matched to what it needs — operator access for repo clone, code and PR, with zero Loki or security surface — and it never makes a security judgment call, deliberately, since that stays Hex's job alone. The level gate keeps the app-error lane as cheap as the security lane: no wake and no turn spent on a quiet 15 minutes.
epics.qa_tests: The gate is deterministic and therefore testable: a quiet 15 minutes produces no wake, and a window containing one ERROR line produces exactly one. What Hex decides once woken is a mind's judgement, read rather than asserted. Argus never auto-merging is the property to verify by trying.

features.title: Ship app logs into Hex's Loki

features.qa_tests: A LogQL query over service=~"hive-.*" returns lines. The existing five sources still flow. One backend, one poller.

stories.acceptance_criteria: App logs arrive with service labels.
stories.qa_tests: A query by service label returns lines from each hive service. The existing sources are unaffected.

features.title: A second classification lane on Hex's existing poller
features.description: Build step two. The existing security loop stays exactly as it is.
features.requirements: Extend netsage_run.py, or a sibling script on the same 15-minute scheduler fire, with a level=~"WARNING|ERROR" LogQL gate over the new app-service labels. Dispatch a wake only when it returns results, same as the existing security gate. This is a new skill sibling to sentinel-triage, not an extension of pick_anomalies()'s regex.
features.acceptance_criteria: One deterministic field per source decides whether to wake Hex — level for app logs, severity for Suricata, PRIORITY for journald — and his skills only run the judgment call on cycles that already cleared that bar.
features.qa_tests: A quiet window produces no wake. A window with one ERROR produces one. The security lane's behaviour is unchanged, which is testable by running it against the same data before and after.

stories.title: Add the level gate as a sibling to sentinel-triage
stories.description: Not an extension of the existing regex heuristic. The structured level field already carries the signal.
stories.requirements: A LogQL filter on level, over the trailing 15 minutes, on the same scheduler fire.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No wake on a quiet window.

features.title: Route app errors to Argus
features.description: Build step three. Next to Hex's existing forward-to-Skippy path.
features.requirements: Security-shaped to Skippy with request_type=security_remediation, as today. App-error-shaped to Argus with request_type=app_error, carrying a correlation id, a log excerpt and the affected service and mind_id. Ambiguous or spanning-both to both, with the same correlation id.
features.acceptance_criteria: Daniel never gets two uncorrelated pings about one incident.
features.qa_tests: A security-shaped finding reaches Skippy only. An app-shaped one reaches Argus only. An ambiguous one reaches both under one correlation id, which is what makes the two pings read as one incident.

stories.title: Add the app_error forward-to-Argus path

stories.acceptance_criteria: Argus receives enough to diagnose without Loki access.
stories.qa_tests: An app_error dispatch carries all four fields. Argus can act on it with no Loki query of its own.

stories.requirements: One id, two dispatches.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Two pings about one incident are recognisably one.
stories.qa_tests: An ambiguous finding produces two dispatches sharing an id.

features.title: Argus, the receiving mind
features.description: Build step four. A receiver, not a poller: no Loki access and no loop of its own. It wakes on a broker message from Hex, diagnoses the named repo or service, proposes a fix, opens a PR through the same stages the orchestrator already runs (step-coding, step-review, step-push-pr), then notifies Daniel via Telegram with a summary, the PR link and an explicit apply-or-hold question. It never auto-merges, and it never makes a security judgment call — deliberately, since that stays Hex's job alone.
features.requirements: Four open questions for Daniel first: confirm the name before scaffolding; choose the deployment — a container, recommended, matching Mordecai's operator-mind pattern with a single /host mount, versus bare-metal systemd like Skippy; decide which repos are in scope for auto-fix-and-PR, all of ~/Storage/Dev or an explicit allowlist starting narrow; and settle the log shipping mechanism, which is shared with the first feature.
features.acceptance_criteria: A forced app error produces a PR and a Telegram notification, and nothing is merged without Daniel.
features.qa_tests: Build step five is the test: force a couple of known app errors through the pipeline and confirm Argus's PR and Telegram notification before trusting it unsupervised. The never-auto-merges property is verified by watching a PR sit until Daniel acts.

stories.acceptance_criteria: He wakes on a message and runs the pipeline.
stories.qa_tests: A broker message wakes him and produces a PR. He holds no Loki credential, which is the scope boundary rather than an oversight.

stories.qa_tests: The PR exists and is unmerged. The notification carries a summary, the link and an explicit apply-or-hold question.

epics.title: Bitcoin Buy-Signal Alerter
epics.description:
A scheduled Ada skill that watches Bitcoin and pings Daniel on Telegram when conditions favour a buy. Daniel is a long-time buy-and-hold accumulator since the four-digit price era — never sells, only buys or sits. The goal is to replace the 'BTC hit some round-number low' app notification with something that fires on signals correlated with historically good accumulation entries.

Why this is the right shape: Daniel already has the CoinGecko API key, the crypto tool is in place, Ada has the skill mounted, and the scheduler natively supports per-skill cron. There is no infrastructure to build — only signal math and threshold tuning. A frontier-model mind on a 60-minute schedule is overkill for the computation itself, but the value is in Ada's judgment about which alerts to suppress and how to phrase them, not in the arithmetic.
epics.requirements:
Constraints: no sell logic, ever — this skill exists to surface buy opportunities and Daniel's pattern is buy and hold, so selling is out of scope. Free data sources only: CoinGecko (already wired, COINGECKO_API_KEY set, free tier plenty for hourly polling) and the alternative.me Fear and Greed Index (no key required). No Glassnode, no paid feeds for v1. Ada owns this end to end: she writes the skill, the cron lives in her SKILL.md frontmatter using schedule and schedule_timezone the same way the existing 3am skill does, and she dispatches alerts via Skippy — Skippy is the only mind that talks to Daniel directly, so Ada hands the alert through hive-comms and Skippy delivers it.

Cadence: hourly is more than enough, since Bitcoin does not move so fast that 15-minute polling buys anything for a multi-year hold, and the free CoinGecko tier is happier with hourly. Recommended 0 * * * * on America/Chicago. Alerts are debounced so Ada does not fire the same threshold every hour for a week straight — once per signal per direction crossing, with the latch reset when the signal moves back above its threshold. Latch state lives in something like minds/ada/data/btc_buy_state.json, carrying per-signal current value, last crossed direction and last alert timestamp.

Out of scope for v1: sell signals; other coins, since this is a Bitcoin skill rather than a portfolio monitor; auto-execution, with no exchange API integration since Daniel clicks through manually; and backtesting — Ada can sanity-check thresholds against historical CoinGecko data once she has coded the signal math, but a real backtest framework is not the goal.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Two tiers keep the noise down and make the alert mean something when it fires. Opportunistic buy fires when any one primary signal crosses its threshold — Mayer Multiple below 1.0, drawdown from ATH greater than 25 percent, or Fear and Greed below 25 — with a light alert tone and a small suggested buy size. Deep value buy fires when two or more signals are stacked, or when price closes below the 200-week MA, with a strong alert tone and a larger suggested size; these are the back-up-the-truck moments. Both tiers include the actual readings in the alert body so Daniel can sanity-check before clicking through to his exchange.
epics.qa_tests: The debounce is the testable part: a signal held past its threshold for a week fires once, not 168 times, and re-arms only when it crosses back. Driven by injected readings and injected time rather than by waiting a week. The alert's phrasing and which alerts to suppress is Ada's judgement, read rather than asserted.

features.title: The four signals
features.description: All four are computable from CoinGecko's free endpoints plus one free sentiment feed.
features.requirements: Mayer Multiple: current price divided by the 200-day simple moving average, computed from coins/bitcoin/market_chart?days=200 — below 1.0 has historically marked deep accumulation zones and the 2.4 upper band has marked overheated tops. Drawdown from all-time high: percent off the ATH, which CoinGecko returns directly in the coin metadata endpoint, so it is essentially free — twenty percent gets your attention, thirty-plus is historically a strong entry for multi-year holders. 200-week moving average: the long-term floor, which Bitcoin has spent very little of its life below and every dip below has been a generational buy; it needs roughly 1400 daily closes against a free-tier max of 365 days, so either cache historical bars locally over time or accept the 365-day Mayer-Multiple substitute for v1 and add the 200W later. Fear and Greed Index: alternative.me's daily 0-to-100 sentiment score, no key required, where under 25 is extreme fear — a classic contrarian buy filter that tends to coincide with capitulation and pairs well as a confirmation overlay on the price-based signals.
features.acceptance_criteria: Three signals work in v1; the 200-week MA is either backed by a local cache or deferred with the substitute named.
features.qa_tests: Each signal computes correctly against known historical readings. The 200-week MA either reads from a cache that has accumulated enough bars, or is absent and the deferral is visible rather than silently returning a wrong figure from 365 days of data.

stories.title: Compute the Mayer Multiple from the 200-day SMA
stories.description: Price over the 200-day simple moving average. Below 1.0 is the deep accumulation zone; 2.4 is the overheated band.
stories.requirements: From coins/bitcoin/market_chart?days=200.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The figure matches a hand calculation.
stories.qa_tests: Against a known price series, the computed multiple matches. A series shorter than 200 days reports insufficient data rather than a figure from fewer bars.

stories.title: Compute drawdown from the all-time high
stories.description: Percent off the ATH, which CoinGecko returns directly in the coin metadata endpoint.
stories.requirements: Essentially free — one metadata call.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Matches a hand calculation.
stories.qa_tests: A known price and a known ATH produce the expected percentage.

stories.title: Pull the Fear and Greed Index
stories.description: alternative.me, 0 to 100, daily, no key required. Under 25 is extreme fear.
stories.requirements: No key, no paid feed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A reading is available every day.
stories.qa_tests: The call returns a reading. A failed call does not take the whole run down — the other three signals still compute.

stories.title: Decide the 200-week MA approach: cache bars or defer
stories.description: Roughly 1400 daily closes needed against a free-tier max of 365 days. Either cache historical bars locally over time, or accept the 365-day Mayer-Multiple substitute for v1 and add the 200W later.
stories.requirements: A decision, with the substitute named if deferred.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The signal is either real or visibly absent, never approximated silently.
stories.qa_tests: If cached, the figure matches a hand calculation once enough bars exist. If deferred, the deep-value tier's price-below-200W condition is absent rather than computed from insufficient data.

features.title: Tiering and debounce
features.description: Two tiers, and a latch that keeps a sustained dip from screaming hourly.
features.requirements: Opportunistic on any one primary signal crossing; deep value on two or more stacked, or price closing below the 200-week MA. Both carry the actual readings. Debounce: once per signal per direction crossing, with the latch reset when the signal moves back above its threshold. Latch state in minds/ada/data/btc_buy_state.json, carrying per-signal current value, last crossed direction and last alert timestamp.
features.acceptance_criteria: A week-long dip produces one alert per signal, not one per hour.
features.qa_tests: Driven by injected readings and injected time: a signal crossing fires once; held past the threshold for a week it stays silent; crossing back and crossing again fires once more.

stories.title: Implement the two tiers with readings in the body
stories.description: Opportunistic on one signal; deep value on two stacked or price below the 200-week MA.
stories.requirements: The actual readings travel in the alert so Daniel can sanity-check before clicking through.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The tier is correct for the signal set.
stories.qa_tests: One crossed signal produces opportunistic. Two produce deep value. The body carries the numbers.

stories.title: Latch each signal so a sustained dip alerts once
stories.description: Once per signal per direction crossing, reset when the signal moves back above its threshold. State in a small JSON file in Ada's data directory.
stories.requirements: Per-signal current value, last crossed direction and last alert timestamp.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No hourly repetition during a sustained dip.

epics.title: Agentic Session Rotation (topic-break trigger)
epics.description:
Long sessions suffer persona drift from context dilution: a mind's own verbose output accumulates and proportionally drowns out the identity and soul priming at the top of the context. Observed live — Mordecai answered one very large question, burned a lot of tokens producing a wall of text, and by the end his personality was gone, reading as generic default Opus; a fresh session on the same mind reads as fully in character. Current rotation only triggers on a token threshold via the Stop-hook rotation_check, which fires too late and for the wrong reason: it reacts to size, not to the conversation actually changing subject.

The idea: add a second rotation trigger, a topic break. When a new inbound message is a genuinely new ask rather than a continuation, rotate to a fresh session before responding, so the new task starts with clean context and full identity, and the existing message becomes turn one of the new session.

Why it is cheap: session rotation already exists end to end. The rotation pipeline wraps the old session and writes a session-memory carry-forward into the next one. So this is a new trigger on existing machinery rather than new rotation code — and the carry-the-in-flight-work-across piece Daniel flagged as tedious is already solved by the carry-forward.
epics.requirements:
Four key design decisions. First, an external doorman rather than mind self-judgment: do not have the bloated mind decide whether the message is a new topic, because by the time the mind reads the message it is already inside the degraded context and has already paid to load it, so its judgment is compromised by the exact thing being escaped. Instead a cheap fast pre-classifier sees only the incoming message and a one-line summary of the current session's topic, and answers continuation or new, running at UserPromptSubmit time before the mind wakes; on new it trips rotation and the message lands as turn one of a clean session, reusing the same local-Ollama structured-call pattern as the insert sweep.

Second, a running topic sentence as incremental state rather than an on-demand lookback: do not have the doorman re-read the whole transcript to figure out the current topic, because that cost grows with session length exactly when you do not want it to. Maintain one short line describing what the session is currently about, refreshed every turn, so the comparison is always O(1) — new message against one sentence — regardless of how long the session runs. Fuse the maintenance into the doorman call rather than making it a separate action: the doorman already runs every turn, so it is a single structured call per turn taking the running topic sentence plus the new message and returning continuation-or-new and the refreshed sentence. On continuation the sentence is gently updated; on new, rotation fires and the sentence resets. Storage is a small per-session topic-sentence file keyed by CLIENT_REF, the same hint-file idiom as the existing rotation-summary file, overwritten each turn and deleted on rotation.

Third, bias conservative: a false new is the dangerous failure because it nukes context the user wanted kept, while a false continuation is benign and leaves the status quo. So only rotate on a confident topic break, and keep an explicit manual override — if the user says new session, always rotate with no classifier vote.

Fourth, mind-agnostic: this lives in the shared session layer, in the rotation pipeline, not bolted onto one body, so it benefits Skippy, Mordecai and the containerised minds equally.
epics.acceptance_criteria: A new ask starts in a clean session with full identity, and a continuation does not. A false continuation is acceptable; a false new is not. The user saying 'new session' always rotates. A free side effect: the running topic sentence is a permanently-current one-line session summary, which can seed the rotation carry-forward instead of generating a fresh summary from scratch at rotation time — one piece of cheap state, two uses.
epics.qa_tests: The model choice needs its own benchmark, and that benchmark is the first real test. The current classifier is gpt-oss:20b-32k, served by the hive-tools container via OLLAMA_CLASSIFY_MODEL — one of the largest models we run, not a small one; the only locally-practical models bigger are the 30-to-33B class and the 120B, and on the A6000 it is not fast. It feels fast today only because the classification it does now, the memory insert sweep, is asynchronous background work fired from the Stop hook, so its latency is never on the user's path and nobody feels the 20B grinding. The doorman is the opposite: a blocking call on the critical path, which must classify the inbound turn before the system knows whether to forward it or spawn a new session, so its wall-clock latency is added directly to time-to-first-token on every message. Reusing the 20B would make every turn wait on one of our heaviest models — exactly the cost the async sweep hides. So measure blocking latency of smaller, newer, similarly-capable models and pick the smallest that still classifies reliably. The job is tiny — restate one line plus one yes-or-no — so a small modern instruct model should match the 20B's accuracy at a fraction of the latency. Candidates worth timing, smallest first: qwen3:4b, granite4:3b, qwen3:8b, lfm2.5 (8.5B), ministral-3:14b. Keep the 20B only if a small model cannot hit acceptable accuracy. The classification quality itself is judged by reading the doorman's calls against real conversation turns, not asserted.

epics.title: Situational awareness across minds: claims, not a log
epics.description:
The incident, 2026-10-06: Skippy stopped ollama.service to copy 333 GB of model blobs to the 2TB drive. Hex detected embeddings failing and escalated it as an outage — correctly, since from where Hex stood it was indistinguishable from one. The escalation reached a different Skippy session, which restarted Ollama mid-copy, not knowing a migration was in flight. Nothing broke, by luck: the copy only read. Two separate defects, one cause — a remediating mind had no way to ask 'is this symptom expected right now?', and the auto-memory recorded the stop as Daniel's action, because nothing in the hive records which actor caused a host event.

What this is not: not a log of what every mind is doing. A feed of activity grows without bound, is noisy, and puts context pressure on every turn in the hive for the benefit of the rare turn that needed it. The useful question is much narrower — is anyone deliberately touching this resource right now? And not a gate: nothing waits for approval and nothing is blocked. A mind that finds a live claim on the resource it was about to remediate reports instead of acting. That is a judgement the mind makes with better information, not a permission check.
epics.requirements:
The primitive is a lease. One broker row: the mind, the host, the resource, one terse line of why, and an expiry. Active claims are injected into every turn through the same UserPromptSubmit hook that already carries standing rules and contextual memory. The property that makes it cheap is that the feed is empty almost always — zero claims is zero tokens — and claims are rare by construction, because the thing being claimed is a shared service being deliberately disturbed, which happens a few times a week.

Why a lease dissolves the hard part: always-injecting spares you teaching a mind when to check, but you still have to teach it to write a claim and, worse, to go back and clear it, and an orphaned claim is permanent noise implying a reconciliation sweep. A lease removes the clearing step as an act of discipline. A claim carries a bounded window stated by the mind when it opens one — thirty to ninety minutes covers nearly everything. It is not renewed automatically: an earlier draft had the per-turn hook renew any claim whose conversation was still alive, which recreates the orphan, because Skippy's sessions run for days so a claim renewed per turn outlives the work that justified it and sits in every mind's context indefinitely. Expiry has to be the one thing nothing can defer. A job that runs longer than its window simply opens another claim — re-claiming is cheap, an immortal claim is not. So it ends two ways: the mind clears it when the work is done, which is courtesy and makes the feed accurate sooner, or the window lapses, which is the guarantee.

The per-turn instruction is stated against the work, never against the claim's existence: if work you started is not finished, renew your claim, or open one if it has already expired; if it is finished, clear it. 'If you have a claim, renew it' is the wrong phrasing and reintroduces the immortal claim, because a mind that spent the night on something else renews a claim for work it abandoned. The mind judges whether the job is still in flight, which is easy — a nine-hour gap between turns is visible in the timestamps, so finding its claim gone is unsurprising rather than alarming.

Why the window still matters once minds renew properly: renewal covers work that outlives its window, but it cannot cover the mind that never gets another turn — a session killed mid-job, a crashed harness, a bounced container. That claim is never renewed and never cleared, and nothing but expiry will remove it. So the window is not there to tidy up after forgetful minds; it is there to survive dead ones. Expiry is the default path, not an error path: there is no sweep because there is nothing to sweep, and the failure mode inverts from 'a claim that lives forever' to 'a claim that expired early' — which leaves the hive in exactly the state it is in today, the status quo rather than a regression.

The write side stays a rule, not a mechanism. Do not try to detect what qualifies as claimable: intercepting systemctl and docker is the ugly glue this is meant to avoid, and it cannot tell a deliberate stop from an incidental one anyway. Instead one line in the standing rules every mind already carries — before stopping, restarting, or relocating the data of a shared service, open a claim. That is the same mechanism that already governs restart behaviour today. Adherence will be imperfect, which is acceptable precisely because the cost of a missed claim is the status quo. Scope is shared resources, not file edits: 'about to modify files' is too wide, since every coding turn modifies files and a feed that is never empty loses the property that makes it free. Claimable means something another mind could observe and misread as a fault — stopping or restarting a service, relocating a service's data, touching another mind's host, taking a shared database down.
epics.acceptance_criteria: Hook placement: the injection goes on UserPromptSubmit, not SessionStart. SessionStart fires once, so a long-running conversation would never see a claim opened after it began — which is exactly the case in the incident. The Stop hook carries the clearing nudge: if you opened a claim and the work is done, clear it. A nudge, not a mechanism, since Stop fires on every turn and work spans many turns, so it cannot know whether the job is finished.
epics.qa_tests: The property to test deliberately is that nothing renews a claim automatically. A claim whose conversation is still alive but whose work finished hours ago must expire, because the per-turn renewal draft is exactly what reintroduced the immortal claim. Expiry is the default path rather than an error path, so there is no sweep to test — there is nothing to sweep.

features.title: Immediate fixes and inputs
features.description: The small items blocking normal use.
features.requirements: Voice via a preset through VOICE_SERVER_URL. Sloan's numeric Telegram user ID added to telegram_allowed_users, which currently holds only Daniel. The skills-dir path pointed at the Codex directory. MIND.md's gateway_url reconciled.
features.acceptance_criteria: Sloan can use Arnold normally, with a voice and a working /help menu.
features.qa_tests: Per story.

stories.title: Wire Arnold's voice through a preset
stories.description: TTS through VOICE_SERVER_URL, preset voice. Note that voice and voice_engine are now fields on the mind rather than a URL per caller, so this should follow that path.
stories.requirements: A preset voice, not a clone.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Arnold speaks.
stories.qa_tests: A reply is spoken in the chosen preset. A voice name the server does not have is refused rather than spoken in a fallback.

stories.title: Add Sloan's Telegram user ID to the allowlist
stories.description: telegram_allowed_users currently holds only Daniel (8776938611). Needs Sloan's numeric ID.
stories.requirements: The ID, then the config change.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Sloan can message Arnold.
stories.qa_tests: Sloan's message is accepted; an unlisted user's is not.

stories.title: Point the skill scan at the Codex skills directory
stories.description: mind_server looks for skills at .claude/skills, the Claude path, but Arnold's skills are Codex at CODEX_HOME/.codex/skills — so the bot /help menu is empty although the harness still uses them.
stories.requirements: The scan reads the Codex directory.
stories.acceptance_criteria: /help lists Arnold's skills.
stories.qa_tests: /help is non-empty and lists the skills the harness actually loads. The current state is the giveaway — the harness uses them while the menu claims there are none.

stories.title: Reconcile MIND.md's gateway_url
stories.description: Currently http://localhost:8433, which is the local bind view. Align it to the LAN IP, or confirm the broker table alone governs routing.
stories.requirements: Either aligned or confirmed irrelevant.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No file claims a URL that would not route.
stories.qa_tests: If the broker table governs, the file's value is documented as cosmetic. If it does not, the LAN IP is in the file and a dispatch reaches it.

stories.title: Revisit Arnold's Codex model now gpt-5.4 is retired
stories.description: gpt-5.4 was set with gpt-5.4-mini for the poll agent. Both are dead on the ChatGPT Codex backend as of 2026-09-11, which the proxy reports as 'Azure API error: 400'.
stories.requirements: A live model for the mind and for the poll agent.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Turns complete rather than 400ing.
stories.qa_tests: A turn completes. A poll agent run completes. A 400 from the proxy on a retired model is the symptom to confirm is gone.

features.title: End-to-end verification
features.description: The three tests that prove the install.
features.requirements: Confirm the broker dispatches to 192.168.5.64:8433 end to end, bind plus firewall. Sloan messages Arnold and one full turn captures, retrieves standing rules and context, and replies in character. Message another mind and confirm poll-task-result delivers the reply.
features.acceptance_criteria: All three pass.
features.qa_tests: The Telegram turn is judged by reading the reply for character and for whether context arrived, not asserted. The reachability test is bind plus firewall across subnets, which is the thing that throws a silent hub-side 500 when the broker row is wrong.

stories.title: Test hub-to-Arnold reachability
stories.description: Confirm the broker dispatches to 192.168.5.64:8433, bind and firewall end to end.
stories.requirements: Cross-subnet, from the hub.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A dispatch arrives.
stories.qa_tests: A hub dispatch reaches the mind server. A wrong or missing broker row throws a silent hub-side 500 with nothing pointing at the cause, so a failure here is diagnosed rather than retried.

stories.title: Run an end-to-end Telegram test with Sloan
stories.description: Sloan messages Arnold; verify one full turn captures, retrieves standing rules and context, and replies in character.
stories.requirements: All three: capture, retrieval, character.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A real turn from Sloan works.
stories.qa_tests: The reply is in character, judged by reading. A lucent row exists for the turn carrying Arnold's UUID. The standing rules and contextual memory are visible in what the reply knows.

stories.title: Run a live inter-mind round trip
stories.description: Message another mind; confirm poll-task-result delivers the reply.
stories.requirements: Outbound and the poller's delivery.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The reply comes back.
stories.qa_tests: A message to another mind produces a reply delivered by the poller, not just a broker 200.

features.title: Discord surface
features.description: Code is done. Ported bots/discord_bot.py, adapted to the bots.* import layout, the COMMS_URL gateway and the discord:{mind_id} namespace, with an async run_discord_bot() coroutine; wired into launch_mind_server_and_bots.py; discord_allowed_users and discord_allowed_channels added to config.py and config.yaml; discord.py recorded in requirements and installed in the venv; imports verified on the box. It auto-disables when DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN is unset, so Arnold stays Telegram-only until configured. Note that the surfaces have since moved to the hive-surfaces package, so this port may be superseded by installing the core instead.
features.requirements: Pending inputs from Daniel: create a Discord application and bot for Arnold and provide the token; provide Daniel's and Sloan's numeric Discord user IDs for discord_allowed_users; enable the Message Content Intent in the Developer Portal; and authorize the bot into Sloan's server via the OAuth2 invite URL, which is a browser click only a Manage-Server user can do.
features.acceptance_criteria: Arnold answers on Discord in Sloan's server, to Sloan and to Daniel.
features.qa_tests: A message in an allowed channel from an allowed user gets a reply. Without the Message Content Intent the bot receives no message text at all, which reads as the bot being broken rather than as a portal setting.

stories.title: Port the Discord bot into Arnold's launcher
stories.description: Done. Adapted imports, COMMS_URL gateway, discord:{mind_id} namespace, async coroutine, allowlists in config, discord.py installed, imports verified. Auto-disables with no token.
stories.requirements: Auto-disable when the token is unset.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Arnold stays Telegram-only until configured.
stories.qa_tests: Imports verified on the box. With no token, the surface does not start and nothing errors.

stories.title: Collect the Discord inputs and bring the surface up
stories.description: A Discord application and bot token for Arnold, Daniel's and Sloan's numeric Discord IDs, the Message Content Intent enabled, and the OAuth2 invite authorized into Sloan's server by a Manage-Server user.
stories.requirements: All four; the invite is a browser click Daniel or Sloan has to make.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Arnold answers on Discord.
stories.qa_tests: An allowed user in an allowed channel gets a reply. Confirm the Message Content Intent is on, since without it the bot sees no text.

features.title: Skill chunks still to port
features.description: Logical groups for toggling. Core comms and identity are installed: send-message-to-mind, the poll-task-result agent, lucent-graph-api, notify and current-time.
features.requirements: Five chunks remain: telemetry hooks, skill lifecycle, reminders, secrets, dev pipeline and info/utility. Each depends on its backing tools being ported, and several are explicitly 'only where its backing tool ships or is ported'.
features.acceptance_criteria: Each chunk is either installed and working or recorded as not applicable with a reason.
features.qa_tests: Per chunk: every skill in it is invocable and its backing tool exists. A skill installed without its tool is worse than an absent one, which is the measured-exclusion rule the Cypher work established.

stories.title: Port the telemetry hooks
stories.description: Restore training_capture and skill_telemetry_capture, the core.* modules, and the tools/stateless/skill_telemetry sidecar the clone lacks. Feeds the learning and skill-recommendation lifecycle.
stories.requirements: Hooks plus modules plus sidecar.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Telemetry flows.
stories.qa_tests: A turn produces a training-capture record and a skill-telemetry record. Note that Nagatha lacks training_capture too, so this is not Arnold-specific.

stories.title: Port the skill-lifecycle chunk
stories.description: skill_manage, skill_curator and skill_proposer tools plus training_turns.db; then install skill-manage, skill-curator, skill-proposer, skill-audit, skill-creator-codex and learn-skill. Depends on the telemetry port.
stories.requirements: Tools first, then the six skills.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The lifecycle runs on Arnold.
stories.qa_tests: A curator pass ages a skill. A proposer pass produces a draft. Both need training_turns.db, so the dependency is real rather than nominal.

stories.title: Port the reminders chunk
stories.description: tools/stateless/reminders, then the reminders, check-reminders and remind-me skills.
stories.requirements: Tool then skills.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A reminder fires.
stories.qa_tests: A reminder set for the near future fires. Driven by injected time where possible rather than by waiting.

stories.title: Port the secrets chunk
stories.description: tools/stateless/secrets, confirm Windows keyring viability, then install the secrets skill. Not required for hive comms — Arnold's tokens live in .env — but included per 'everything'.
stories.requirements: Windows keyring viability confirmed first.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Either working or recorded as unviable on Windows with a reason.
stories.qa_tests: A secret round-trips through the Windows keyring. If it cannot, that is the finding rather than a broken install.

stories.title: Port the dev-pipeline chunk
stories.description: Backing tools as needed, then orchestrator, story-start, story-close, planning-genius, code-genius, code-review-genius, master-code-review, git, github-push, tool-creator and update-documentation, plus the step-* Codex agents. Note the Planka teardown orphaned several of these, so the replacement work-item source has to be settled first.
stories.requirements: A live work-item source before the pipeline skills are installed.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No skill installed against a deleted tool.
stories.qa_tests: Each installed pipeline skill completes against a real work-item source. Installing one that calls the deleted planka.py is the failure to avoid.

stories.title: Port the info and utility chunk
stories.description: weather, crypto-price, x-search, x-ai-lurker, browse, agent-logs, sitrep, send-email, home-assistant, planka, design-session, mermaid-diagram-creator and moderate — each only where its backing tool ships or is ported.
stories.requirements: Only where the backing tool exists. home-assistant needs an HA token Arnold may not have, and planka's tool is deleted.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Every installed skill works; every excluded one is excluded on a measured gap.
stories.qa_tests: Each installed skill completes. Each exclusion is backed by a check on the box rather than an assumption — the measured-exclusion rule.
